_note: Coarse ontology used to compare confusion across datasets whose vocabularies range from 6 to 198 classes. Each fine-grained class is assigned by substring match, first rule wins, and anything unmatched falls to 'other'. Edit freely: a novel vocabulary will land largely in 'other' until rules are added for it.
_provenance: Nine super-categories as described in the paper. The research script make_supercat_confusion.py defined only seven plus 'other'; 'electronics' and 'barricades' were reconstructed from the 267-class vocabulary on 2026-09-04 per the authors, with barricades covering AV2 and nuScenes road-side objects. Validated: barricades->person reproduces the paper's 12% exactly, and storage->table its 0.22. 'other' is retained as a catch-all; the paper implies a complete manual assignment of all 267 classes, so residual differences (storage diagonal 0.59 vs 0.61, overall cross-category rate 0.129 vs 0.15) are consistent with classes that still fall to 'other' here.
_overrides_note: Exact per-class assignments applied BEFORE the substring rules. Needed where a class name contains a substring belonging to another super-category: 'message_board_trailer' is road-side signage, not a vehicle, and 'mobile_pedestrian_crossing_sign' is a sign, not a person.
